abstract: |
  This note examines whether volatility on the local equity market has increased, how it relates to offshore economic and policy uncertainty, and what this means for building risk ballasts into local equity funds. Local volatility has become more episodic since 2020 rather than permanently higher, and its spikes are largely imported: global implied volatility and oil price volatility explain close to three quarters of the monthly variation in Capped SWIX volatility, while local currency volatility adds little. The SafeCore fund has outperformed its benchmark but has not been a risk ballast: its volatility matches the market's, two gold miners carry almost half of its risk, and its quality-momentum style has no low-volatility tilt. The opportunity for stock selection, measured by dispersion and correlation, was weak from 2022 to 2024 but has improved since 2025, and rising bond and currency volatility have tended to precede less rewarding conditions for stock pickers.
---

Idx_Daily            <- read_rds("data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")

# Introduction \label{Introduction}

A recent seminar argued that oil price volatility and global policy uncertainty are spilling over into local equity markets, and that local portfolios should lean more towards lower-volatility stocks. This note tests that argument in three steps. Part A establishes whether local volatility has increased and whether it mirrors the global experience. Part B evaluates how the SafeCore fund has navigated volatility and what its factor exposures are. Part C studies dispersion and correlation, to gauge the alpha opportunity in the market since 2020.

# Part A: Has local volatility increased? \label{PartA}

## Data

Local index returns (Capped SWIX, Top 40, Mid Caps and Small Caps, in rand) are available from January 2015, so the analysis runs from January 2015 to September 2026. The global comparison uses total return indexes in US dollars: MSCI ACWI, MSCI Emerging Markets, the S&P 500, the Euro Stoxx 50 and the Nikkei 225. To link volatility to uncertainty, the analysis uses implied volatility (VIX, V2X, VXEEM), economic policy uncertainty (EPU) indexes, US bond market volatility (MOVE), Brent oil volatility and currency volatility (SAVI for USDZAR and JP Morgan's global FX volatility index).

Two data issues were treated. The global and European EPU indexes are monthly values repeated on every day, so all comparisons with them are done at a monthly frequency. The SAVI index is quoted as a decimal rather than a percentage on 109 days (mostly March to June 2021); these values were rescaled.

## Realised volatility

Figure \ref{rollvol} plots the rolling three-month realised volatility of each index, with every other index shown in grey for context. The shaded bands mark five market events: two South African political shocks (Nenegate in December 2015, and the March 2017 cabinet reshuffle followed by the sovereign downgrade to junk) and three global shocks (the COVID-19 crash, the 2022 Ukraine war and oil price shock, and the April 2025 US tariff shock). The COVID-19 crash dominates every series, with local volatility peaking above 50%. Outside of 2020, local volatility has been punctuated by shorter spikes, most of which coincide with the global events.

```{r rollvol, fig.height = 6.8, fig.cap = "Rolling 3-month realised volatility: each panel highlights one index against all others (grey) \\label{rollvol}"}
Plot_Roll_Vol(Roll_Vols)
```

Figure \ref{calvol} shows the same story by calendar year. The notable recent feature is 2026: Capped SWIX volatility (about 21% year-to-date) is well above that of developed markets (MSCI ACWI about 12%) and much closer to emerging markets (MSCI EM about 25%). Local volatility in 2025-26 is therefore tracking the emerging market experience rather than the developed market one.

```{r calvol, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Calendar-year realised volatility (\\%) \\label{calvol}"}
Plot_Calendar_Vol(Cal_Vols)
```

Figure \ref{regime} compares average volatility before and after 2020, and the share of days each index spends in a high-volatility state (above its own long-run 80th percentile). Including the COVID period, every index shows higher volatility after 2020. Once the COVID crash is excluded, however, average Capped SWIX volatility barely rises (from 15.4% to 16.0%), while the share of high-volatility days still increases (from 17% to 22%). The increase in local volatility is therefore better described as **more frequent volatility episodes** than as a permanently higher level. It is also smaller than the increase seen in developed markets such as the S&P 500 and the Nikkei.

```{r regime, fig.height = 4.8, fig.cap = "Average rolling volatility and share of high-volatility days, before and after 2020 \\label{regime}"}
Plot_Vol_Regimes(Vol_Regimes_Long(Roll_Vols))
```

## Home-grown or imported volatility?

Figure \ref{events} measures how far rolling volatility rose around each event, from the level just before the event to its peak during the event and the following month. The two local political shocks were short-lived: Nenegate lifted local volatility by about 6 percentage points, roughly three times the global move, but the 2017 reshuffle and junk downgrade barely moved local volatility at all, suggesting the downgrade was largely priced in. The three global shocks, by contrast, lifted local volatility by about as much as global volatility (roughly 8 to 9 points in 2022 and 2025, and close to 40 points during COVID-19). The large volatility episodes in the local market have therefore been imported, while home-grown political shocks have been smaller and faded quickly.

```{r events, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Rise in rolling 3-month volatility around each event \\label{events}"}
Plot_Event_Vol(Event_Vol_Long(Roll_Vols, Q1_Events))
```

## Does local mirror global?

Figure \ref{rollcor} shows rolling one-year correlations between weekly Capped SWIX returns and the global indexes. Weekly returns are used because the JSE closes before US markets open, which biases daily correlations downward. The correlation with MSCI ACWI averages around 0.68 and rose to roughly 0.9 during the COVID crisis: in a global sell-off, local and global markets move together, exactly when diversification is needed most. More recently the correlation with emerging markets has fallen, suggesting that part of the 2026 volatility is local or EM-specific.

```{r rollcor, fig.cap = "Rolling 52-week correlation of Capped SWIX with global indexes (weekly returns) \\label{rollcor}"}
Plot_Roll_Cor(Roll_Cors)
```

## Conditional volatility

Ljung-Box tests on squared returns strongly reject the null of no ARCH effects for all three series (p-values close to zero), confirming volatility clustering. Comparing information criteria, the asymmetric GARCH models fit better than the standard GARCH, so a GJR-GARCH(1,1) is used with an AR(1) mean and skewed-t errors. Table \ref{tab:garch} reports the key parameters and Ljung-Box tests on the standardised residuals: the squared standardised residuals show no remaining clustering (p-values of 0.71-0.99), confirming that the model captures the volatility dynamics. Two results stand out. First, the symmetric shock parameter ($\alpha$) is close to zero while the leverage parameter ($\gamma$) is large: volatility rises after bad news but hardly reacts to good news. Second, persistence is high (about 0.97 locally), implying a half-life of a volatility shock of roughly a month. Local volatility shocks fade faster than global (MSCI ACWI) shocks but slower than shocks to the broad EM index.

```{r garchtab, results = "asis"}
Garch_Out$Params %>%
    left_join(Garch_Diagnostics(Garch_Out$Fits), by = "Name") %>%
    rename(Index = Name, alpha = alpha1, beta = beta1, gamma = gamma1, `Half-life (days)` = HalfLife_days,
           `LB p (z)` = `LB p-value (z)`, `LB p (z squared)` = `LB p-value (z^2)`) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = "GJR-GARCH(1,1) parameters (AR(1) mean, skewed-t errors) and Ljung-Box (12 lags) p-values for the standardised residuals \\label{tab:garch}", Digits = 3)
```

```{r sigma, fig.cap = "GJR-GARCH conditional volatility, annualised \\label{sigma}"}
Plot_Garch_Sigma(Garch_Out$Sigma)
```

## How much of local volatility is imported?

The rolling correlation above uses a fixed 52-week window. A DCC-GARCH model (Engle, 2002) instead updates the correlations every week from the latest shocks. It is fitted to weekly returns of the Capped SWIX, MSCI ACWI and MSCI EM: each series has its own GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student-t errors, and a DCC(1,1) process with a multivariate t distribution models the correlations of the standardised residuals. Table \ref{tab:dcc} shows that the correlation dynamics are significant and persistent (a half-life of about 16 weeks), while the asymmetric aDCC finds no asymmetry ($g$ = 0.00, likelihood-ratio p = 1.00): correlations respond to the size of joint shocks, crash and rebound alike, rather than only to joint falls.

Because the model gives the full conditional covariance matrix $H_t$, the share of local conditional variance explained by the two global indexes can be computed every week, as $h_{lg,t}' H_{gg,t}^{-1} h_{lg,t} / h_{ll,t}$ (the R-squared of local on global returns, using that week's covariances). Figure \ref{dcc} colours local conditional volatility by this imported share. On average about half (52%) of local variance moves with global markets. The share reaches two-thirds (65%) in the COVID crash but falls to 46% during Nenegate, and it rises with the level of volatility: the bigger the episode, the more of it is imported. The 2022 oil shock is an exception, with only about half of local variance moving with global markets, possibly because the resource-heavy local market reacted differently to the commodity-price spike.

```{r dcctab, results = "asis"}
Q1A_DCC_Table(Fit_DCC, Fit_aDCC) %>%
    select(Model, a = `a (shock)`, b = `b (memory)`, `g (asym.)` = `g (asymmetry)`, `Half-life (wks)` = `Half-life (weeks)`,
           `Log-lik.` = `Log-likelihood`, AIC, `LR p-value` = `LR test p-value`) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = "DCC and asymmetric DCC (aDCC) models of weekly Capped SWIX, MSCI ACWI and MSCI EM returns \\label{tab:dcc}", Digits = 3)
```

```{r dcc, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "Capped SWIX conditional volatility from the DCC model, coloured by the share of local variance explained by global markets \\label{dcc}"}
Plot_DCC_Imported(Imported)
```

## What drives local volatility?

Figure \ref{drivers} overlays monthly local GARCH volatility (standardised) on each uncertainty measure, and Figure \ref{heat} reports their correlations. Local volatility moves closely with market-based measures of fear: global equity volatility (correlation of 0.87 with MSCI ACWI volatility), implied volatility (about 0.8 with VIX, V2X and VXEEM) and oil volatility (0.70). By contrast, the news-based policy uncertainty indexes show almost no correlation with local volatility (0.08 for global EPU). Policy uncertainty appears to matter for markets only once it shows up as a shock to global risk appetite or to oil prices.

```{r drivers, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Local volatility vs uncertainty measures (monthly, z-scores) \\label{drivers}"}
Plot_Drivers_Z(Monthly_Panel)
```

```{r heat, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Correlation of monthly volatility and uncertainty measures \\label{heat}"}
Plot_Cor_Heatmap(Monthly_Panel)
```

Table \ref{tab:reg} formalises this with a regression of standardised local volatility on the offshore measures. Standard errors are Newey-West, because persistent monthly volatility series leave autocorrelated residuals. The VIX and oil volatility are the dominant and highly significant drivers, and the offshore measures alone explain about 73% of the monthly variation in local volatility. Adding local currency volatility (SAVI) barely changes the fit and is not significant. Global EPU enters negatively once the VIX is controlled for, but it is only borderline significant (p = 0.04) and loses significance when SAVI is added; as EPU and the VIX are correlated, this coefficient should be read with caution.

```{r regtab, results = "asis"}
Driver_Regs$Coefs %>%
    mutate(term = gsub("[.]+", " ", term) %>% trimws()) %>%
    select(Model, Variable = term, Beta = estimate, `Std. error` = std.error, `t-stat` = statistic, `p-value` = p.value) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = paste0("Standardised regression of Capped SWIX GARCH volatility on uncertainty measures (monthly, Newey-West standard errors). R-squared: ",
                                 paste(Driver_Regs$Fit$Model, round(Driver_Regs$Fit$R2, 2), sep = " = ", collapse = "; "),
                                 " \\label{tab:reg}"), Digits = 2)
```

## Implications for Part A

Local volatility has not risen to a permanently higher level, but volatility episodes have become more frequent since 2020, and in 2025-26 local volatility has tracked emerging markets rather than developed markets. These episodes are largely imported: global risk-off shocks and oil price volatility explain most of the variation, the share of local variance that moves with global markets rises from about half in normal times to two-thirds in a global crash, and volatility rises far more after losses than after gains.

Was the seminar right that oil price volatility and global policy uncertainty are spilling into local equities? Partly. Oil volatility clearly feeds into local volatility, but policy uncertainty only seems to matter once it turns into global market fear. For local equity funds, the practical takeaway is that the risk worth protecting against is a global sell-off rather than a rand shock, so any risk ballast (lower-volatility stocks, rand-hedge exposure) should be judged on how it holds up in those episodes. That is the lens used to evaluate SafeCore in Part B.

Three caveats apply. The regressions capture associations rather than causal effects. Monthly volatility measures are persistent, which is why Newey-West standard errors are used; with about 140 monthly observations, the borderline EPU result should still be read with caution. Finally, local volatility is measured in rand and global volatility in US dollars, so part of any gap between them, and part of the imported share from the DCC model, reflects currency movements rather than the equity markets themselves.

```{r data-load-B}
Stock_Rets    <- read_rds("data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
Index_Const   <- read_rds("data/Index_Constituents.rds")
Factor_Scores <- read_rds("data/Factor_Scores.rds")
Hedge_Plays   <- read_rds("data/Currency_Hedge_Plays.rds")
STeFI         <- read_rds("data/STeFI_Index.rds")

SC_Holdings   <- Q1B_SafeCore_Holdings(read_rds("data/SafeCore.rds"), Index_Const)
LowVol_Rets   <- Q1B_LowVol_Rebuild(Index_Const, Stock_Rets)
B_Panel       <- Q1B_Return_Panel(Build_Portfolio(SC_Holdings, Stock_Rets, "SafeCore"), LowVol_Rets, Idx_Daily)
Risk_Contrib  <- Q1B_Risk_Contrib(SC_Holdings, Stock_Rets)
Own_Scores    <- Q1B_Own_Scores(Stock_Rets, Factor_Scores)
Active_Exp    <- Q1B_Active_Exposures(Q1B_Port_Exposures(Q1B_All_Scores(Own_Scores, Factor_Scores), SC_Holdings, Index_Const))
```

# Part B: Does SafeCore navigate volatility? \label{PartB}

SafeCore is constructed without any explicit view on volatility, so the question is whether it nonetheless behaves like a risk ballast, and if not, why. The analysis first establishes *whether* it navigates volatility well, then *where* its volatility comes from, and finally *what kind of fund* it is in terms of factor exposures. The Capped SWIX (J433) is the benchmark throughout.

## Data and a "risk ballast" reference

SafeCore's daily returns are built from its month-end holdings and daily stock returns from 2015, with weights rescaled to 100% (at least 95% of the fund's weight has return data in every month) and allowed to drift between rebalances. As a reference for what a low-volatility strategy achieves, the Low Vol index is rebuilt from its constituents with quarterly rebalancing (end of March, June, September and December), which extends it from 2024 back to September 2020. Over 2024-2026, where the two overlap, the rebuild has a daily correlation of 0.995 with the actual index and a tracking error of 1.4% a year, which is accurate enough to use it for the earlier years.

## Performance through volatility

Table \ref{tab:score} summarises the trade-off. SafeCore has been a good fund in return terms: since 2015 it returned 11.4% a year against 8.7% for the benchmark, with an information ratio of about 0.5. But it has not reduced risk. Its volatility equals the benchmark's, its beta is close to one, and since 2020 its maximum drawdown was deeper than the benchmark's. The rebuilt Low Vol index lowered volatility as intended, but at a large cost in return over a strong market period, and without a smaller drawdown.

```{r scoretab, results = "asis"}
bind_rows(
    Q1B_Scorecard(B_Panel %>% filter(Name != "Low Vol"), STeFI, as.Date("2015-01-01"), as.Date("2026-09-30")) %>% mutate(Period = "2015-2026"),
    Q1B_Scorecard(B_Panel, STeFI, as.Date("2020-09-01"), as.Date("2026-09-30")) %>% mutate(Period = "Sep 2020-2026")
) %>%
    mutate(across(c(`Ann. return`, `Ann. vol`, `Max drawdown`, `Tracking error`), ~ .x * 100)) %>%
    select(Period, everything()) %>%
    Print_Table(Caption = "Risk and return scorecard vs the Capped SWIX (returns, volatility, drawdown and tracking error in \\%; Sharpe ratio uses STeFI as the risk-free rate) \\label{tab:score}", Digits = 2)
```

Figure \ref{growth} shows where the outperformance came from and what it did not change: SafeCore pulled ahead in 2016-2018 and again from 2020 (since when it has tracked the Top 40 closely), but in every major sell-off it fell about as far as the market. Figure \ref{volratio} makes the point directly: SafeCore was less volatile than the benchmark in only about a quarter of rolling one-year windows, and has been slightly more volatile since 2021. The Low Vol index was smoother in every window, by about 8% on average.

```{r growth, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Growth of R100 and drawdowns \\label{growth}"}
Plot_Growth_DD(Q1B_Growth_DD(B_Panel))
```

```{r volratio, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Rolling 1-year volatility of SafeCore and the Low Vol index against the Capped SWIX \\label{volratio}"}
Plot_Vol_Ratio(Q1B_Vol_Ratio(B_Panel))
```

Figure \ref{capture} shows how each fund participates in market moves. SafeCore's yearly points cluster around (1, 1): in most years it simply captures all of the market's upside and all of its downside, with only 2016 and 2017 in the ideal quadrant and 2019 and 2024 in the worst. The Low Vol index sits in the bottom-left, capturing only 80-88% of both up and down moves: a genuine low-beta strategy reduces both sides symmetrically rather than offering free downside protection.

```{r capture, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Up- and downside capture vs the Capped SWIX by calendar year \\label{capture}"}
Plot_Capture(Q1B_Capture(B_Panel))
```

The stress tests in Figure \ref{stress} and the regime analysis in Figure \ref{regimes} confirm that SafeCore's edge is not protection. It beat the benchmark in 7 of 10 stress episodes, but mostly by less than 1.5 percentage points, and it did worse in the most relevant episode for the seminar's argument, the 2022 oil shock. Its excess return is similar across calm, normal and stressed VIX regimes (about 0.2% a month), and it beats the benchmark in only half of stressed months: SafeCore's outperformance is a steady stock-selection edge, not a volatility-management one.

```{r stress, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Cumulative returns in stress episodes \\label{stress}"}
Plot_Stress(Q1B_Stress_Returns(B_Panel, Q1B_Stress_Windows(Q1_Events, Implied_Vol, N_VIX = 5)))
```

```{r regimes, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Monthly excess return over the Capped SWIX by VIX regime \\label{regimes}"}
Plot_VIX_Regimes(Q1B_VIX_Regimes(B_Panel, Implied_Vol))
```

## Sources of volatility

A stock's share of a fund's risk can differ greatly from its weight, because risk depends on its volatility and on how it co-moves with the other holdings. SafeCore's variance is therefore decomposed into stock and sector contributions each month (Euler risk contributions, using a Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance matrix estimated over the previous year). Figure \ref{sectorrisk} shows that resources have always been an important source of risk, and this has become more prevalent recently: in August 2026 they made up 40% of the fund but 68% of its risk (Figure \ref{waffle}). Figure \ref{lollipop} identifies the culprits: AngloGold Ashanti and Gold Fields together carry almost half of the fund's risk, while banks and industrials (Standard Bank, Absa, FirstRand, MTN, Naspers) contribute less risk than their weight and act as diversifiers.

```{r waffle, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Share of SafeCore's weight vs share of its risk by sector, latest month (each square = 1\\%) \\label{waffle}"}
Plot_Risk_Waffle(Risk_Contrib)
```

```{r sectorrisk, fig.cap = "Sector contributions to SafeCore's risk \\label{sectorrisk}"}
Plot_Sector_Risk(Risk_Contrib)
```

```{r lollipop, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Weight vs share of risk, top 10 risk contributors \\label{lollipop}"}
Plot_Weight_vs_Risk(Risk_Contrib, TopN = 10)
```

Two structural features amplify this (Figure \ref{conchedge}). SafeCore is concentrated: its effective number of stocks (17-22) is about half that of the Capped SWIX, and it has fallen in 2026, so a few stocks can dominate its risk. And it holds fewer pure rand hedges and rand-neutral stocks than the benchmark, but more rand plays, alongside currency-sensitive "rand leverage" miners. This is not a profile that cushions a global risk-off shock, which Part A showed to be the main source of local volatility.

```{r conchedge, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Concentration (left) and rand-hedge profile at the latest date (right) \\label{conchedge}"}
Plot_Conc_Hedge(Q1B_Effective_N(SC_Holdings, Index_Const), Q1B_Hedge_Profile(SC_Holdings, Index_Const, Hedge_Plays))
```

## Factor exposures

Two scores are constructed from price data at each month-end. Momentum is the return from six months to one month ago (skipping the latest month, whose short-term reversals would add noise), and low volatility is minus the stock's six-month realised volatility, so that a high score means a low-volatility stock. Both are standardised across stocks each month and capped at $\pm 3$ to limit the influence of illiquid stocks with extreme moves.

Figure \ref{scores} compares them with the third party's scores. The own momentum score agrees well with the vendor's (an average rank correlation of about 0.6); the largest disagreements are the gold and platinum miners, which the vendor still rates as high-momentum, suggesting it uses a longer look-back. The own low-volatility score, by contrast, is essentially unrelated to the vendor's "Volatility Sensitivity" (rank correlation of about 0.1), and further checks show the vendor measure is also barely related to realised volatility or market beta. It appears to capture sensitivity to *changes* in market volatility rather than the level of volatility, so it should not be read as a low-volatility score.

```{r scores, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "Own vs third-party factor scores \\label{scores}"}
Plot_Score_Compare(Q1B_Score_Agreement(Own_Scores, Factor_Scores), Own_Scores, Factor_Scores, SC_Holdings)
```

To contextualise SafeCore, the stock scores are aggregated into composite portfolio scores (weighted averages over each portfolio's holdings) for SafeCore and the Value, Momentum, Quality and Low Vol indexes. Because the vendor's scores turn out to be benchmark-relative (the Capped SWIX scores almost exactly zero on every vendor factor), all exposures are expressed relative to the Capped SWIX. The factor indexes line up with their labels, which validates the approach. Against them, SafeCore's fingerprint (Figure \ref{finger}), whose shape is closest to the Momentum and Quality indexes and furthest from Low Vol, is that of a quality-momentum fund with a mild value tilt and no low-volatility tilt at all. Figure \ref{drift} adds the timing: SafeCore's momentum exposure rose sharply in 2026 while its low-volatility exposure turned negative, which is how the fund drifted into the volatile gold miners that now dominate its risk.

```{r finger, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "Factor fingerprints: active exposures vs the Capped SWIX, last 12 months (dashed outline = SafeCore) \\label{finger}"}
Plot_Fingerprint(Active_Exp, Months = 12)
```

```{r drift, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "SafeCore's active factor exposures over time \\label{drift}"}
Plot_Factor_Drift(Active_Exp)
```

## Implications for Part B

SafeCore has been a good fund, but not a risk ballast. It outperformed its benchmark by close to 3% a year, yet with the same volatility, near-full participation in market falls and no consistent advantage in stressed periods. Its volatility is concentrated in a handful of resource stocks, its effective breadth is half the benchmark's, and its momentum tilt has recently pulled it further into these names. If the team wants SafeCore to offer some protection in the global risk-off episodes identified in Part A, practical steps would be to budget risk rather than only weights (capping single-stock and sector risk contributions), to monitor the momentum tilt for crowding into one theme, and to add an explicit low-volatility tilt or sleeve, accepting, as the Low Vol index shows, that this costs some upside in strong markets.

```{r data-load-C}
Monthly_CSV <- Q1C_Monthly_CSV(Q1C_Daily_CSV(Q1C_Constituents(Index_Const, IndexName = "Capped SWIX")))
Pair_Cor    <- Q1C_Roll_PairCor(Index_Const, IndexName = "Large Caps", Window = 63)
Opportunity <- Q1C_Opportunity(Monthly_CSV, Pair_Cor)
Realised    <- Q1C_Realised_Spreads(Index_Const)
Macro_Vars  <- c("VIX", "VXEEM", "Oil Vol", "MOVE (US bond vol)", "EPU Global", "JPM Global FX vol", "SAVI USDZAR vol")
Macro_Panel <- Q1C_Macro_Panel(Unc_Levels, Opportunity, Monthly_CSV, Pair_Cor, Vars = Macro_Vars)
```

# Part C: The alpha opportunity since 2020 \label{PartC}

Active managers often add value when stocks behave differently from one another. The alpha opportunity is therefore measured from two complementary angles: dispersion (how far apart stock returns are on a given day) and correlation (how much stocks move together over time). High dispersion with low correlation describes a stock-picker's market; low dispersion with high correlation a macro-driven one. Constituent data is available from August 2020.

## Dispersion

Dispersion is measured as the daily cross-sectional volatility (CSV) of the Capped SWIX constituents, weighted by their previous-day index weights:
$$CSV_t = \sqrt{\sum_i w_{i,t-1}(R_{i,t} - \bar{R}_t)^2}$$
where $\bar{R}_t$ is the weighted average (index) return. The weighted measure is preferred because it reflects the opportunity relevant to a fund benchmarked against the Capped SWIX, where a large move in a stock with a negligible index weight matters little, and because the unweighted measure is dominated by small, illiquid stocks with erratic prices. Two corporate-action artefacts were removed before the calculation (the listing of Richemont's shareholder warrants in November 2020, which shows a one-day "return" of over 369,000%, and the Fortress A/B share restructure in February 2024); the warrant print alone would otherwise have tripled November 2020's dispersion.

Figure \ref{csv} shows that dispersion was high in late 2020, fell to its lowest level in 2024 (an average daily CSV of about 1.6%) and has risen again to about 2.0% in 2026. The unweighted measure follows the same pattern at a higher level. Figure \ref{decomp} splits the weighted variance exactly into a within-sector part (the stock-picking opportunity) and a between-sector part (the sector-allocation opportunity). Until 2024 about 80% of dispersion came from within sectors; since 2025 the between-sector share has risen sharply, to about a third on average in 2026 and half in some months. This mirrors Part B: resources, and gold miners in particular, have moved very differently from the rest of the market, so sector calls now matter as much as stock selection.

```{r csv, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Cross-sectional volatility of Capped SWIX constituents \\label{csv}"}
Plot_CSV(Monthly_CSV)
```

```{r decomp, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Within- vs between-sector share of dispersion \\label{decomp}"}
Plot_CSV_Decomp(Monthly_CSV)
```

## Correlation

Figure \ref{paircor} shows the distribution of pairwise correlations between Large Cap stocks over rolling 63-day windows. Showing the median and the middle 50% of pairs, rather than a single average, reveals whether all stocks were moving together or only some. Correlations peaked in 2022, the year of the Ukraine war and aggressive rate hikes, when the whole distribution shifted upwards, and fell to their lowest levels in 2024-2025, when stocks traded more on their own fundamentals.

```{r paircor, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Rolling pairwise correlations of Large Cap stocks \\label{paircor}"}
Plot_PairCor(Pair_Cor)
```

## Mapping the alpha opportunity

Dispersion and correlation are only weakly related in this sample (a correlation of 0.17), so they capture different aspects of the opportunity. Figure \ref{quad} plots them against each other: 2022 sits in the macro-driven half of the map, 2023-2024 in the low-dispersion half, and many months of 2025-2026 in the stock-picker's quadrant. The map is summarised with an Alpha Opportunity Index, equal to standardised dispersion minus standardised correlation (Figure \ref{oppindex}). The opportunity was strong in late 2020 and early 2022, weak from mid-2022 to 2024, and has improved markedly since 2025.

```{r quad, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Monthly dispersion vs average pairwise correlation \\label{quad}"}
Plot_Opp_Quadrant(Opportunity)
```

```{r oppindex, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Alpha Opportunity Index \\label{oppindex}"}
Plot_Opp_Index(Opportunity)
```

To check that the index reflects a real opportunity, Figure \ref{realised} compares it with two payoffs available in the data: the return gap between the best and worst quintile of Capped SWIX stocks each month, and the gap between the best and worst factor index. In high-opportunity months the stock-quintile spread averaged 26% a month, against 22% in low-opportunity months (a correlation of 0.51 with the index), whereas the factor spread is small and only weakly related. The index therefore captures a genuine stock-selection opportunity, though it says little about style timing.

```{r realised, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Return spreads by level of the Alpha Opportunity Index \\label{realised}"}
Plot_Realised(Opportunity, Realised)
```

## Alpha opportunity and global macro factors

Figures \ref{leadlag} and \ref{macroreg} relate dispersion, correlation and the opportunity index to the global macro measures from Part A. Higher equity fear (VIX, VXEEM) raises dispersion, but it also raises correlation, and predicts higher correlation the following month, so its net effect on the opportunity is small: prices spread out, but increasingly in response to the same risk-on/risk-off swings. Bond and currency volatility are what hurt stock pickers. High US bond volatility (MOVE) goes with lower dispersion and higher correlation and has the strongest negative relationship with the opportunity index; global FX and rand volatility show the same pattern. These measures are also more strongly related to *next* month's opportunity than to this month's, so rising rate and currency volatility act as an early warning of a more correlated, less rewarding market, as in 2022. Policy uncertainty (EPU) again shows little relationship, consistent with Part A.

```{r leadlag, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Same-month and next-month correlation of macro measures with dispersion, correlation and the opportunity index \\label{leadlag}"}
Plot_LeadLag(Q1C_LeadLag(Macro_Panel, Macro_Vars))
```

```{r macroreg, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Dispersion and correlation in low vs high macro regimes \\label{macroreg}"}
Plot_Macro_Regimes(Q1C_Macro_Regimes(Macro_Panel, Macro_Vars))
```

These macro relationships are correlations estimated on about six years of monthly data and are sensitive to a few episodes (2022 in particular), so they should be read as indicative rather than causal. The quintile spread is also a foresight measure: it shows how much there was to gain from stock selection, not what any manager actually earned.

# Conclusion \label{Conclusion}

The three parts give a consistent picture. Local volatility has not moved to a permanently higher level, but volatility episodes have become more frequent and are largely imported, through global risk-off shocks and oil price volatility. SafeCore has added return but has not protected investors in those episodes: its risk is concentrated in a few resource stocks and its quality-momentum style has no low-volatility tilt. Meanwhile, the opportunity to add value through stock selection has improved since 2025, although more of it now comes from sectors moving apart, and rising bond and currency volatility have tended to signal tougher conditions for stock pickers. The implication for the team is that SafeCore can keep its stock-selection edge while building in a risk ballast aimed at the shocks that actually drive local volatility: limiting single-stock and sector risk, adding a low-volatility tilt, and monitoring global rate and currency volatility as early warnings.
